morphology.summary: Not an organelle in the classical sense but the structure that defines every cell, bacterial, archaeal or eukaryotic: a selectively permeable phospholipid BILAYER, about 5-10 nm thick, that separates the cell's interior from the outside world. It is built from thousands of amphipathic phospholipid molecules that self-assemble into two stacked sheets (leaflets) with their water-loving heads facing the two watery compartments (extracellular fluid outside, cytoplasm inside) and their water-fearing tails buried against each other in the middle, out of contact with water. Studded and floating within this lipid sea are proteins (integral/transmembrane and peripheral), cholesterol, and - on the outer face only - a coat of sugar chains, the glycocalyx. The whole assembly is a fluid, dynamic mosaic, not a rigid wall: the Singer-Nicolson 'fluid mosaic model' (1972) describes lipids and proteins as free to drift laterally within their own leaflet.
morphology.kind: the boundary membrane common to ALL cells (bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes alike) - a lipid bilayer, not a rigid cell wall and not an organelle with its own genome
morphology.size: About 5 nm thick in reality (roughly 6-10 nm is also cited depending on stain/technique) - astonishingly thin: a human red blood cell, ~8 um across, is already about 1000x wider than its own membrane is thick. The poster figure uses a representative 15 um extent for the illustrated patch/cell, per the project's scale data; the membrane itself is drawn at the nanometre scale as a cutaway slab, not literally to that ratio (no illustration could keep a 5 nm membrane visible at a 15 um scale bar).
morphology.shape: Best shown as a flat or gently curved CUTAWAY SLAB seen edge-on, so the bilayer reads as two parallel rows of round heads with a tail-filled middle band between them - the classic cross-section view - rather than as a whole rounded cell (which would make the 5 nm membrane too thin to show any internal detail).
morphology.phospholipid_molecule: Each phospholipid is amphipathic: one round, water-loving (hydrophilic) HEAD (a phosphate-containing group) and, hanging from it, two long, water-fearing (hydrophobic) fatty-acid TAILS. In the bilayer, phospholipids arrange tail-to-tail: two leaflets, each one molecule thick, sit back-to-back so that ALL the tails - from both leaflets - meet and mingle in an oily middle layer with no water, while ALL the heads face outward into water on both sides. This tails-together, heads-outward arrangement is the single most important thing to get right: it is the entire reason the structure exists (it is the lowest-energy way to hide hydrophobic tails from water) and the thing illustrations most often get backwards.
morphology.outer_leaflet: The half of the bilayer facing the extracellular fluid (outside the cell). Its phospholipid heads point outward into the watery extracellular space. This is also the ONLY face that carries the glycocalyx sugar chains and the only face many receptor/ID proteins present their business end toward.
morphology.inner_leaflet: The half of the bilayer facing the cytoplasm (inside the cell). Its phospholipid heads point inward into the watery cytosol. Carries NO glycocalyx - the asymmetry between outer and inner leaflets (different lipid species, no sugar coat inside) is a real, well-documented feature of real membranes, not an illustrator's simplification.
morphology.hydrophobic_core: The oily, water-free middle zone of the bilayer where the fatty-acid tails of both leaflets meet and interdigitate. About 3-4 nm of the total ~5 nm thickness. This is the barrier that makes the membrane impermeable to ions and most water-soluble molecules, which is exactly why dedicated channel and pump proteins are needed to cross it.
morphology.integral_proteins: Proteins permanently embedded in the bilayer, their hydrophobic membrane-spanning stretches (often alpha-helices of 20-25 amino acids) sitting amid the lipid tails. Many are TRANSMEMBRANE, crossing the full thickness and exposed on both faces (single-pass, or multi-pass with up to a dozen membrane-spanning segments folded back and forth). Functionally these are the channels, pumps, carriers and receptors: e.g. a channel protein forms a continuous water-filled PORE straight through the bilayer that lets specific ions or molecules cross without touching the hydrophobic core.
morphology.peripheral_proteins: Proteins that are NOT embedded in the lipid tails at all. They attach loosely to only ONE face of the membrane - either by binding to the exposed part of an integral protein or by a direct but non-penetrating association with the polar lipid heads. They can be pulled off without disrupting the bilayer itself, unlike integral proteins. Found on both the outer and the inner face (e.g., cytoskeletal anchor proteins on the inner face).
morphology.cholesterol: In animal cells, small hydrophobic cholesterol molecules are wedged in between the phospholipid tails, oriented parallel to them. Cholesterol is a fluidity BUFFER: at high temperature it restrains excessive movement of the fatty-acid tails (making the membrane less fluid/more ordered); at low temperature it prevents the tails from packing too tightly and freezing solid (keeping the membrane fluid). It sits within the hydrophobic core/tail region, not among the heads.
morphology.glycocalyx: A fuzzy coat of carbohydrate chains (oligosaccharides) covalently attached to membrane lipids (making glycolipids) and, more abundantly, to membrane proteins (making glycoproteins). CRITICAL ASYMMETRY: the glycocalyx exists ONLY on the outer/extracellular face of the membrane - never on the cytoplasmic face. It is highly hydrophilic, attracts a water shell to the cell surface, and its specific sugar-chain patterns act as a molecular ID badge/barcode that lets other cells (including the immune system's NK cells) tell 'self' from 'non-self' or recognise a particular cell type. It is also exactly the kind of surface feature that pathogens including viruses exploit as a docking receptor.
morphology.fluidity_note: The membrane is FLUID, not a rigid wall or solid shell: individual phospholipids and most proteins are free to drift laterally within their own leaflet (this is why it is called the fluid mosaic model, Singer & Nicolson 1972). Illustrations must avoid making it look like a static brick wall or an immobile crystalline lattice - the heads and tails should read as densely packed but not rigidly gridded, and nothing should look welded in place.
morphology.colour_note: A real membrane has no intrinsic colour - it is essentially colourless/transparent, ~5 nm thick, far below the wavelength of visible light. All colour in a teaching illustration (distinct tints for heads vs tails vs proteins vs cholesterol vs glycocalyx) is a teaching convention chosen for legibility, not the structure's real appearance.

structures.note: Round, water-loving head of an outer-leaflet phospholipid, facing the extracellular fluid. Part of the top row of heads in a cutaway view.

Round, water-loving head of an inner-leaflet phospholipid, facing the cytoplasm. Part of the bottom row of heads in a cutaway view - must clearly mirror the outer row, not be missing or different in kind.

structures.de: Hydrophobe Schwänze (treffen sich in der Mitte)
structures.note: The fatty-acid tails of both leaflets, pointing INWARD and meeting/interdigitating in the oily core between the two rows of heads. THE key structural point: tails must point at each other, never outward into the water.

A protein spanning the full thickness of the bilayer, exposed on both faces, with a visible water-filled channel/pore running through its centre. Sits fully embedded among the lipid tails, not resting on top.
A protein attached to only ONE face of the membrane (resting on the surface / bound to an integral protein's exposed part), never penetrating into the hydrophobic tail region.
Small, compact hydrophobic molecules wedged in among the phospholipid tails, oriented parallel to them; a fluidity buffer, not a head-region structure.

Branching sugar chains attached to outer-leaflet proteins/lipids, projecting out into the extracellular space. MUST appear ONLY on the outer face - never on the cytoplasmic/inner face. This asymmetry is what makes NK-cell 'self/non-self' recognition and virus-receptor docking possible.

do_not_draw: Do NOT draw a single layer of molecules. The membrane is ALWAYS a BIlayer: two stacked leaflets of phospholipids, tail-to-tail.

Do NOT point the hydrophobic tails outward into the water. Tails must point INWARD and meet each other in the middle; heads must point outward into the watery extracellular fluid and cytoplasm. Getting this backwards is the single most common and most serious error for this subject.
Do NOT draw the glycocalyx sugar chains on the inner/cytoplasmic face. They belong ONLY on the outer face. Sugar chains on both faces, or on the inner face only, are both scientifically wrong.

Do NOT draw the membrane as a rigid brick wall, a solid crystalline lattice, or a completely uniform gridded pattern. It is FLUID (the fluid mosaic model) - components drift; the illustration should read as a busy but soft, non-rigid mosaic, not an engineered lattice.
Do NOT draw a solid, unbroken shell/sheet with no visible molecular substructure - the heads-tails-heads sandwich structure must be legible, especially in the textbook/3d cutaway views.

Do NOT add a rigid cell wall (peptidoglycan mesh, cellulose wall, or a thick capsule) outside the membrane. This subject is the plasma membrane of a generic/eukaryotic cell, not a bacterial or plant cell - no bacterial or plant wall structures.
Do NOT stud the membrane with ribosomes. Ribosomes studding a membrane surface signify the rough endoplasmic reticulum, a different organelle - not appropriate here.

Do NOT draw integral/transmembrane proteins floating loose on the surface, or peripheral proteins buried in the tail region - integral proteins must cross through the hydrophobic core; peripheral proteins must sit only on one surface.
Do NOT draw the channel protein as solid/without a visible pore - at least one integral protein should show a clear passage/channel through its centre.

Do NOT anthropomorphise it (no face, eyes or limbs) in the textbook/sem/3d/watercolor plates - that belongs only on the separate coloring-book page. No baked-in text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows or watermarks in any scientific plate.

colour_legend.head_inner_leaflet: #4A90A4 same teal-blue as the outer heads (same molecule type, same colour, to visually tie the bilayer together as one lipid class) - distinguished only by position (bottom row)
colour_legend.hydrophobic_tails: #F2D98D (pale warm gold/cream), the oily middle band between the two rows of heads
colour_legend.integral_protein: #C0392B (warm brick red) spanning the full slab thickness, with a visible pale channel/pore through the centre
colour_legend.peripheral_protein: #7FB37F (soft green), resting on one face only
colour_legend.cholesterol: #8E6BAF (dusty violet) small compact wedges among the tails
colour_legend.glycocalyx: #E8B93A (golden yellow) branching chain shapes projecting from the outer face only
colour_legend.note: The membrane has no colour in life; all colour is a teaching convention chosen to make the bilayer/protein/cholesterol/glycocalyx relationships legible at a glance, and especially to make the outer-vs-inner asymmetry (glycocalyx only outside) visually unmistakable.

sources.title: Freeze-fracture / intramembrane particles background
sources.note: Freeze-fracture splits the membrane along its hydrophobic mid-plane; transmembrane proteins then appear as particles (intramembrane particles, IMPs) studding the exposed fracture face - basis for choosing a freeze-fracture EM as the real reference and for describing what its granular texture represents.
